title: Pelvic Floor Muscle Training
summary:
The pelvic floor is a network of muscles, fasciae, and ligaments that supports the bladder, uterus, and rectum, helps control urine and stool, and contributes to sexual function and lumbopelvic stability. Pregnancy overloads it through uterine weight, hormonal changes (relaxin and estrogens), and posture and breathing changes, and vaginal delivery can stretch the muscles and damage nerves.

Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) is described as the first line of noninvasive prevention and treatment. It targets strength, endurance, fast contractions, coordination, and relaxation. The chapter sets out a four-phase program, example exercises, adaptations by fitness level, and precautions, and ends by stressing education, supervision, and daily routines to keep women adhering to the program.
points: The pelvic floor has three muscle layers: the deep pelvic diaphragm (levator ani), the middle urogenital diaphragm, and the superficial perineal layer.
Estimated prevalence of dysfunction in pregnancy and postpartum: urinary incontinence 30-50%, pelvic organ prolapse 10-20%, fecal incontinence 4-10%, pelvic pain or dyspareunia 20-40%.
Strength training uses maximum sustained contractions of 3-10 s, 8-12 repetitions, two to three sets a day.
Endurance training uses submaximal contractions of 20-40 s; fast contractions are sets of 10 lasting 1-3 s.
Phase 1 (weeks 1-4) is awareness: 3-s contractions with 6 s relaxation, 10 repetitions, twice a day.
Phase 2 (weeks 5-12) is 8-s maximum contractions, 10 repetitions, 3 sets, plus 10 sets of 2-s fast contractions, 5-7 days a week.

Phase 3 (second and third trimesters) applies contractions to coughing, lifting, and position changes, with inhale = relax and exhale = contract; Phase 4 continues daily PFMT for at least 6 months postpartum.
An initial assessment with the PERFECT test (Power, Endurance, Repetitions, Fast, Every Contraction Timed) is recommended, with strength graded 0 to 5.
Sedentary women focus on awareness and short contractions, active women do three to five sets a day, and athletes prioritize relaxation and avoid perineal overtraining.
takeaways: Start PFMT in the first trimester and train daily for 10-15 min.
Practice relaxing the pelvic floor as much as contracting it.
Breathe in to relax and breathe out to contract, and combine with diaphragmatic breathing.
Contract before lifting weights or coughing.
Avoid compensating with the glutes or abdomen when learning the contraction.
Continue postpartum for at least 6-12 months.
cautions: Consult your obstetrician if there is a threat of preterm labor or placenta previa.
Avoid PFMT with acute pelvic pain or uterine contractions during exercise.
Avoid PFMT with vaginal infections or unhealed postpartum wounds.
